title: Routing Subspaces: Auditing Evaluation-to-Deployment Mismatch in Fine-Tuned Language Models
claim: A behavioral gap is carried by one linear coordinate, so shifting or suppressing it along that axis merges the two framings.
layout: 4 panels, left-to-right, shared 1-D axis, arrows showing interventions
description: Four scatter-plot panels share a horizontal axis labeled d̂_L. Panel (a), 'two clusters', shows orange ordinary-use points on the left and blue evaluation points on the right. The cluster means are marked μ^dep and μ^eval, with a thick black arrow d_L between them and a green diamond marking the zero midpoint. Panel (b), 'remove evaluation', has a blue arrow labeled −λσd̂_L. The blue points shift left and overlap the orange ones, while the original positions stay as faint gray dots. Panel (c), 'add ordinary use', has an orange arrow labeled +λσd̂_L. The orange points shift right to overlap the blue ones. Panel (d), 'joint intervention', collapses both groups onto a vertical dashed green line at zero. Dashed arrows point inward, and the label ⟨h, d̂_L⟩ → 0 appears below. A legend at the bottom maps the colors: blue is evaluation framing, orange is ordinary-use framing, gray is pre-intervention, and green is the suppressed coordinate. The eye goes first to the panel (a) clusters and the bold arrow.
caption: Schematic of the routing-coordinate audit. (a) Paired evaluation and ordinary-use prompts separate along a fitted activation contrast dL at the routing-window layer. (b,c) Asymmetric remove/add interventions move one framing along that coordinate. (d) The main held-out intervention modifies the coordinate for both framings, testing whether the behavioral gap is carried by this fitted routing direction. Figure 4 reports the cross-family intervention matrix.
abstract: Safety evaluations often assume that behavior observed during testing reflects behavior in ordinary use, but fine-tuning can break this assumption. A checkpoint can appear fixed under evaluation-style prompts while the same behavior persists under ordinary-use prompts. Output scores reveal this mismatch but do not locate it. We investigate whether the distinction is encoded in a stable internal site and introduce an audit that fits a paired activation contrast at a path-patching-informed mid-depth window, then modifies the resulting coordinate on held-out prompts. The intervention reduces the evaluation-to-deployment gap by more than $0.12$ in ten of twelve model--behavior settings and closes it (post-intervention gap below $0.06$) in four, across four full-matrix instruction-tuned model instances; among the eight settings with $n{\geq}120$ paired questions, six reduce and one closes. A fifth model supports localization and edit-provenance checks, and in the twelve settings deployment-framed rates change by at most $6.1$pp. On retrained checkpoints, random directions at the same dose do not reproduce the effect, and off-window controls do so only in part. The strongest literal evidence for an evaluation-versus-deployment distinction comes from sandbagging, whose prompt framing is explicitly evaluative; sycophancy and refusal test framing-contingent task distinctions. The two weak cells, both sycophancy, show where a single-coordinate audit at a fixed window is not sufficient. The audit is a non-adaptive, white-box diagnostic for controlled fine-tuned checkpoints, not a training-time defense, a guarantee of deployment safety, or evidence about naturally arising failures.
